rv.q: Already this new comedy about the Queen Mother and her longtime butler, William Tallon, has made me laugh more than any other play this year.

It is also a gift for all who admire superlative acting, as Wilton, a dame far less in the spotlight than her colleagues Dame Judi and Dame Maggie, gives a customarily magnificent performance in which humour and pathos are woven sinuously together.
Penelope Wilton is magnificent.
There’s something gleefully subversive about Dos Santos’s script and Grandage’s bouncy production, which makes it compelling.

Emily Barber memorably doubles up as a sitcom actress and a bonkers aristo. But my abiding memory is of the QM serenely holding a dildo-shaped sculpture made by a fake African prince. It’s all just froth - but there’s a dash of bitters at the end to keep this comic cocktail from cloying.
Grandage’s production executes itself as nimbly as clockwork, delivering plenty of laughs along with the live corgis.
As adult-oriented Carry On comedy it's reasonably good fun.
But even if it can’t pull everything together, it’s still bubblingly witty.
Grandage’s production is consistently funny, and the performances entertain, but this play really doesn’t know what it’s saying.
It’s amusing, and toys gingerly with social issues, among them the peculiarly British business of class divide and deference.
The writing has sophistication and some jokes are funny but this is the epitome of theatre as light entertainment.
Backstairs Billy is pure entertainment at its finest.
Wilton and Evans are a delightful duo, bouncing off each other effortlessly.
That it can make for theatre by turns devastating and delicious is among its major achievements, too.
Minor blemishes aside, this is a glorious evening’s entertainment.
This impeccably played comedy of manners nicely balances palace gossip with broader ideas about class, power, and way that tradition can both comfort and stifle.
Penelope Wilton and Luke Evans proffer a partnership to relish that those corgis can’t begin to compete with.
Backstairs Billy, for all its humour, feels like a smudged snapshot rather than a fully realised portrait.
This right royal romp is uproariously funny but also gives a fascinating insight to the inner workings of that famous family.
It is both but not quite fully either.
Alas, it comes too late and leaves a sour taste even if, for much of its length, we are amused.

cn.t: Wilton and Evans shine in this witty but uneven comedy about the Queen Mother and her devoted servant Billy Tallon. Critics praise the laughs and performances, though some find the script lacks depth and purpose.
